name: Gregory of Sinai
knownFor: A monk, tonsured on Mount Sinai, who taught the prayer of the mind to the monks of Mount Athos and built monastic houses in the paroria, the borderlands, of Macedonia. His chapters on prayer, stillness and the signs of grace and delusion stand in the Philokalia.
dates: The Philokalia's editors say he flourished about 1330, under an emperor Andronikos, and give no birth or death year. Philipp Meyer, in 1894, places the bringing of the prayer of the mind to Athos in the thirteenth century, after a tradition he takes from the Life by the patriarch Kallistos. No witness gives the year of his death.
place: Mount Sinai, where the notice says he became a monk. Crete, where Meyer says he learned the prayer of the mind. Mount Athos, at the skete of Magoula, opposite Philotheou in the notice and a cell of Iviron in Meyer. The paroria, the borderlands, of Macedonia, where the notice says he built three lauras; Rački names a mountain Paroria near Adrianople.
role: Monk and teacher of the prayer of the mind; founder of the lauras of Paroria

keyWorks.title: Chapters in acrostic, and other chapters
keyWorks.about: short teachings on the commandments, prayer and the signs of grace and of delusion. The Philokalia printed them in 1782, and Migne reprinted them, with a Latin version, in Patrologia Graeca 150.

keyWorks.title: On stillness and the two ways of prayer
keyWorks.about: fifteen chapters on the two ways into prayer of the mind. Printed after it are his short pieces on how the hesychast, the monk of stillness, should sit at prayer (on a stool, bent low, gathering the mind into the heart) and how to say the prayer. Some teach it with the mouth and some with the mind, he writes, and he teaches both.

keyWorks.title: To Longinus, on stillness and prayer
keyWorks.about: where he writes that even those baptized as grown men may feel it only in the water, and not in the Spirit.

traces: Franjo Rački, retelling Kallistos's Life of Theodosius of Trnovo in 1869, names among Gregory's disciples Kallistos, later patriarch of Constantinople, and Jacob, later archbishop of the Serbs, and tells of Theodosius at Paroria.
Basil of Poiana Marului wrote a preface for those who wish to read his book. It is printed among the writings of Paisius Velichkovsky's circle.
Nil Sorsky, in his Tradition and Rule, cites him often. He repeats that Gregory taught watchfulness to the monks in communities as well as to hermits.
Paisius Velichkovsky's own chapters on mental prayer cite him, and Paisius says he composed hymns to the Trinity sung every week and a canon to the Cross.
remembered: The Philokalia's notice calls him the common teacher of holy watchfulness, who still leads by his writings.

A later Life of Maximus the Hut-burner, printed in the 1893 Philokalia in everyday Greek, tells how Gregory asked Maximus whether he kept the prayer of the mind. At the end Gregory no longer called him a man, but an angel on earth.

uncertain: Most of the story comes from a short notice by the editors of the Philokalia, which Migne reprinted in 1865. The notice names a longer Life by his disciple, the patriarch Kallistos. Meyer and Paisius Velichkovsky, archimandrite of Neamț in Moldavia, cite that Life, and Paisius says the Greek copy which reached his community was incomplete and lacked the account of Gregory's death.

Whether anyone on Athos knew the prayer. The notice names three monks at Magoula who gave a little time to contemplation. Paisius Velichkovsky, citing Kallistos's Life, says Gregory found no one with even a little knowledge of it. Meyer makes the three Gregory's pupils.
When and where he died. None of the witnesses gives the year or the place.
When he flourished. The notice says about 1330. Meyer places the coming of the prayer of the mind to Athos in the thirteenth century.
Where he learned the prayer of the mind. Meyer alone says Crete, from a hermit named Arsenios.
What Paroria was. Migne's Latin takes the word to mean the borders of Macedonia. The 1893 Philokalia prints it as a place name, and Rački names a mountain Paroria near Adrianople.

Whether the Athos fathers opposed him. Basil of Poiana Marului, in his preface to the chapters of Philotheos of Sinai, says the most learned fathers of Athos at first did. The notice says only that the monks did not know the terms.
